summary: Defines new naming constraints for well-known Kerberos principal names and well-known Kerberos realm names. It updates RFC 4120 and is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: In a big company with name tags, some names are reserved for special jobs. This sets aside special names so nobody uses them wrongly.

questions: what is a well-known kerberos principal name
what happens when a kerberos well-known name is not supported
subtitle: Reserves 'WELLKNOWN' Kerberos names for special meanings and says what servers must do when they do not support one.

tldr.problem: Kerberos has no reserved names, so a protocol that wants a special principal or realm name (such as the anonymous one) can collide with an ordinary account and accidentally grant it access.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a well-known principal name type, KRB_NT_WELLKNOWN, whose first component is WELLKNOWN, and a WELLKNOWN realm name type. If a well-known name is used but not supported, authentication must fail with a defined error code.
tldr.outcome: Servers that do not understand a well-known name reject it rather than treat it as an ordinary name. The RFC updates RFC 4120 and sets up two IANA registries for such names.

today: RFC 6111 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4120. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Reserved Names Are Needed
sections.content:
Protocol designers sometimes need a Kerberos principal name or realm name to carry a special meaning instead of naming one particular instance. The example in the RFC is the anonymous principal name and anonymous realm name from the Kerberos anonymity support in RFC 6112. That name pair says only that the client's identity is not disclosed.

RFC 4120 has no reserved names. Designers have so far picked names that are very unlikely to be in use, but nothing stops a deployed implementation from letting someone create an account with the same name, and then access could be granted unexpectedly. The realm name space in RFC 4120 is reserved, but no name is defined and the RFC does not say what happens with an unknown reserved realm name.

This RFC fixes both gaps by defining well-known names and the behavior required when one is used but not supported.
sections.eli5: Imagine a class where a kid could sign up with the name 'Teacher'. This RFC says special names are reserved, and anyone who does not know a special name must say no.

sections.title: Well-Known Principal Names
sections.content:
A new name type, KRB_NT_WELLKNOWN, with value 11, marks well-known principal names. Such a name MUST have at least two KerberosString components, and the first component MUST be the literal string WELLKNOWN.

If a well-known principal name is used as the client or server principal name but is not supported, the Authentication Service (AS) and the application server MUST reject the attempt. The Ticket Granting Service (TGS) is more relaxed: it MAY reject an unsupported well-known client name and SHOULD reject an unsupported well-known server name. The RFC explains that this allows incremental updates and easier migration, for example letting a cross-realm ticket-granting ticket work when not every realm on the path has been updated.

Anywhere else in a Kerberos message, an unsupported well-known principal name makes authentication fail with KRB_AP_ERR_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN (82). No error data is defined for it.
sections.eli5: Special names all start with the same secret word, WELLKNOWN. If a computer sees that word and does not know the special name, it turns the visitor away.

sections.title: Well-Known Realm Names
sections.content:
RFC 4120 allows realm names of the 'other' style. This RFC defines a realm type WELLKNOWN as a name of that style, written WELLKNOWN:realm-name.

The rejection rules mirror those for principals. The AS and application server MUST reject an unsupported well-known client or server realm. The TGS MAY reject an unsupported well-known client realm and SHOULD reject an unsupported well-known server realm. Elsewhere in a message, authentication MUST fail with KRB_AP_ERR_REALM_UNKNOWN (83).

Unless otherwise specified, every principal name inside a well-known realm is reserved. If such a name is used but not supported and the attempt is rejected, the error code MUST be KRB_AP_ERR_PRINCIPAL_RESERVED (84).
sections.eli5: Whole special neighborhoods can be reserved too. Every address inside one is off limits unless the rules say otherwise.

sections.title: Error Codes and the Transited Field
sections.content:
Three new error codes carry no accompanying error data: KRB_AP_ERR_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN (82), KRB_AP_ERR_REALM_UNKNOWN (83) and KRB_AP_ERR_PRINCIPAL_RESERVED (84).

RFC 4120 has the TGS add the previous realm to the transited field of the ticket it returns. Well-known realms normally carry special meaning and do not stand for intermediate realms on the client's path, so unless otherwise specified the TGS MUST NOT put a well-known realm name in the transited field. Parties checking the transited path MUST reject a path that includes one. A KDC that checks the path therefore MUST NOT set the TRANSITED-POLICY-CHECKED flag in the resulting ticket.

The DOMAIN-X500-COMPRESS encoding treats realm names as strings, so it can still be used when a reserved realm is the client or server realm. If the client's realm is well-known, the abbreviation forms that build on the preceding name cannot be used at the start of the transited encoding, and the null-subfield form cannot be used next to a well-known realm.
sections.eli5: A special neighborhood is never listed as a stop on the trip itself. If someone's trip log says it was, the guard must refuse it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because RFC 4120 reserves no names, a well-known name can collide with a normal one, and accidental reuse MUST be avoided. If an unsupported well-known name were accepted, access could be granted unintentionally.

The RFC's example: a KDC supports this specification but not the anonymous authentication of RFC 6112, and allows a principal to be created with the anonymous principal's name. If that principal is given access to resources and the KDC later supports anonymous authentication, anonymous users could inadvertently reach those resources. Requiring KDCs to reject unknown well-known names reduces this risk.

A well-known name created before the KDC was updated SHOULD be renamed. Account provisioning code MUST be updated so it does not create principals with unsupported well-known names.
sections.eli5: If a stranger could sign up as 'Anonymous' and get a key, then real anonymous visitors might later walk into places that stranger had access to. So special names must always be refused when not understood.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: This RFC is only a framework for defining well-known names. It does not define any specific well-known principal or realm itself. Two new IANA registries hold well-known Kerberos principal names and realm names defined under it. The evaluation policy for each is 'Specification Required', as described in RFC 5226.
sections.eli5: There are now two official lists of the special names, and you need a written document to add a name to them.

items.label: KRB_AP_ERR_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN
items.desc: A well-known Kerberos principal name is used but not supported.

items.label: KRB_AP_ERR_REALM_UNKNOWN
items.desc: A well-known Kerberos realm name is used but not supported.

items.label: KRB_AP_ERR_PRINCIPAL_RESERVED
items.desc: A reserved Kerberos principal name is used but not supported.
